section.paragraph: Now, to use Formula (5), we need to evaluate the definite integral

But we do not have the algebraic rule defining the integrand $$c$$ for all values of $$t$$ in $$\lbrack 0,28\rbrack$$ . In fact, we are given its values only at a set of discrete points in that interval. In situations such as this, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus proves useless because we cannot find an antiderivative of $$c$$ . (We will complete the solution to this problem in Example 4.)

Other situations also arise in which an integrable function has an antiderivative that cannot be found in terms of elementary functions (functions that can be expressed as a finite combination of algebraic, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions). Examples of such functions are

Riemann sums provide us with a good approximation of a definite integral, provided that the number of subintervals in the partitions is large enough. But there are better techniques and formulas, called quadrature formulas, that give a more efficient way of computing approximate values of definite integrals. In this section, we look at two rather simple but effective ways of approximating definite integrals.
section.heading: The Trapezoidal Rule
section.paragraph: We assume that $$f(x) \geq 0$$ on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ to simplify the derivation of the Trapezoidal Rule, but the result is valid without this restriction. We begin by subdividing the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals of equal length $$\Delta x$$ , by means of the $$\left( {n + 1} \right)$$ points $$x_{0} = a,x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n} = b$$ , where $$n$$ is a positive integer (Figure 3).

The horizontal axis x ranges from a to b with tick marks labeled a = x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3, ellipsis, x_n minus 1, x_n = b. the vertical axis y is unlabeled. The curve labeled y = f(x), starts at the top left of the viewing window away from the y axis, slopes downward, concave up, decreasing to the right, reaches its low point, slopes upward, inflects, concave down, increasing to the right, plateaus and continues to slope downward to the right to exit the first quadrant on the right of the viewing window. The region below the curve is segmented by the perpendiculars dropped from the path of the curve to the tick marks x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3, x_n minus 1, and x_n each in the x axis. The region between the tick marks a = x_0 and x_1 is labeled R_1, x_1 and x_2 is labeled R_2, x_2 and x_3 labeled is R_3, x_n minus 1 and x_n = b is labeled R_n.

section.paragraph: Then the length of each subinterval is given by
$$\Delta x = \frac{b - a}{n}$$
Furthermore, as we saw earlier, we may view the definite integral

as the area of the region $$R$$ under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ between $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ . This area is given by the sum of the areas of the $$n$$ nonoverlapping subregions $$R_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{n}$$ , where $$R_{1}$$ represents the region under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$x = x_{0}$$ to $$x = x_{1}$$ , and so on.

The basis for the Trapezoidal Rule lies in the approximation of each region, $$R_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{n}$$ by a suitable trapezoid. This often leads to a much better approximation than one obtained by means of rectangles (a Riemann sum).

Let’s consider the subregion $$R_{1}$$ , shown magnified for the sake of clarity in Figure 4. Observe that the area of the region $$R_{1}$$ may be approximated by the trapezoid of width $$\Delta x$$ whose parallel sides are of lengths $$f\left( x_{0} \right)$$ and $$f\left( x_{1} \right)$$ . The area of the trapezoid is given by
$${\left\lbrack \frac{f\left( x_{0} \right) + f\left( x_{1} \right)}{2} \right\rbrack \Delta x} {{Average of the lengths of the parallel sides} \times {width}}$$

The curve enters from the top left of the viewing window, slope downward, concave up, deceasing to the right and exits on the right of the viewing window. Two perpendiculars are dropped from the path of the curve to the tick marks x_0 and x_1 with height f(x_0) and f(x_1) respectively. The region between the two perpendiculars with horizontal width of delta x is shaded and labeled R_1.

figure.caption: The area of $$R_{1}$$ is approximated by the area of the trapezoid.

section.paragraph: Similarly, the area of the region $$R_{2}$$ may be approximated by the trapezoid of width $$\Delta x$$ and sides of lengths $$f\left( x_{1} \right)$$ and $$f\left( x_{2} \right)$$ . The area of the trapezoid is given by
$$\left\lbrack \frac{f\left( x_{1} \right) + f\left( x_{2} \right)}{2} \right\rbrack \Delta x$$
Continuing, we see that the area of the last ( $$n$$ th) approximating trapezoid is given by
$$\left\lbrack \frac{f\left( x_{n - 1} \right) + f\left( x_{n} \right)}{2} \right\rbrack \Delta x$$
Then the area of the region $$R$$ is approximated by the sum of the areas of the $$n$$ trapezoids—that is,

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left\lbrack \frac{f{(x_{0})} + f{(x_{1})}}{2} \right\rbrack \Delta x + \left\lbrack \frac{f{(x_{1})} + f{(x_{2})}}{2} \right\rbrack \Delta x + \ldots + \left\lbrack \frac{f{(x_{n - 1})} + f{(x_{n})}}{2} \right\rbrack \Delta x} \\ { = \frac{\Delta x}{2}\left\lbrack {f{(x_{0})} + f{(x_{1})} + f{(x_{1})} + f{(x_{2})} + \ldots + f{(x_{n - 1})} + f{(x_{n})}} \right\rbrack} \\ { = \frac{\Delta x}{2}\left\lbrack {f{(x_{0})} + 2f{(x_{1})} + 2f{(x_{2})} + \ldots + 2f{(x_{n - 1})} + f{(x_{n})}} \right\rbrack} \end{array}$$
Since the area of the region $$R$$ is given by the value of the definite integral we wished to approximate, we are led to the following approximation formula, which is called the Trapezoidal Rule.

section.heading: Simpson’s Rule
section.paragraph: Before stating Simpson’s Rule, let’s review the two rules we have used in approximating a definite integral. Let $$f$$ be a continuous, nonnegative function defined on the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . Suppose the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ is partitioned by means of the $$n + 1$$ equally spaced points $$x_{0} = a,x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n} = b$$ where $$n$$ is a positive integer, so that the length of each subinterval is $$\Delta x = {\left( {b - a} \right) \slash n}$$ (Figure 5).

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed in the first quadrant of an x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis x ranges from a to b with tick marks labeled a = x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3, ellipsis, x_n minus 1, x_n = b. The vertical axis y is unlabeled. The curve starts away from the origin between the axes, concave down, increasing to the right, inflects, concave up, increasing to the right, inflects steeply, concave down, increasing to the right, inflects, concave up, slopes to the right, concave down, decreasing to the right and exits the first quadrant at the top right of the viewing window. The region below the curve is segmented by the perpendiculars dropped from the path of the curve to the tick marks x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3, x_n minus 1, and x_n each in the x axis. The region between the tick marks a = x_0 and x_1 is labeled R_1, x_1 and x_2 is labeled R_2, x_2 and x_3 labeled is R_3, x_n minus 1 and x_n = b is labeled R_n.

figure.caption: The area of the region under the curve is equal to the sum of the areas of the $$n$$ subregions $$R_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{n}$$ .

section.paragraph: Let’s concentrate on the portion of the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ defined on the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ . When we use a Riemann sum to approximate the definite integral, we are in effect approximating the function $$f(x)$$ on $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{1}} \right\rbrack$$ by the constant function $$y = f\left( p_{1} \right)$$ , where $$p_{1}$$ is chosen to be a point in $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{1}} \right\rbrack$$ ; and we are approximating the function $$f(x)$$ on $$\left\lbrack {x_{1},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ by the constant function $$y = f\left( p_{2} \right)$$ , where $$p_{2}$$ lies in $$\left\lbrack {x_{1},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ . Using a Riemann sum, we see that the area of the region under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ between $$x = x_{0}$$ and $$x = x_{2}$$ is approximated by the area of the region under the approximating “step” function (Figure 6a).

image.alt: Details Two graphs a and b plots a curve each in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. In both the graphs, the horizontal axis x has three tick marks labeled x_0, x_1, and x_2 respectively from left to right. The horizontal axis y is unlabeled. The first graph a labeled the area of the region under the curve is approximated by the area of the rectangles. The horizontal axis has two tick marks labeled p_1 and p_2, which form the midpoint between the tick marks x_0 and x_1, x_1 and x_2 respectively. The curve starts in the first quadrant, slopes upward to the right, then the curve concaves down, increasing to the right, inflects, concave up, increasing to the right and exits the first quadrant at the top right of the viewing window. Two vertical rectangles are graphed in the region below the curve with the horizontal width of x_0 to x_1 and x_1 to x_2 respectively and vertical height of f (p_1) and f (p_2) respectively. The curve cuts the top left corner of the two rectangles, passes through the midpoint of the top width at (p_1, f (p_1)) and (p_2, f (p_2)). The region enclosed by the rectangles is shaded. The second graph b labeled the area of the region under the curve is approximated by the area of the trapezoids. The curve starts in the first quadrant, slopes upward to the right, reaches a closed circle at (x_0, f(x_0)), then the curve concaves down, increasing to the right, inflects at (x_1, f(x_1)), continues to slope upward, reaches another closed circle at the coordinate (x_2, f(x_2)). Thereafter the curve concave up, increasing to the right and exits the first quadrant at the top right of the viewing window. A perpendicular is dropped to the x axis from the coordinates (x_0, f(x_0)), (x_1, f(x_1)), and (x_2, f(x_2)) each to the x axis, forming two trapezoids in the region below the curve, with a horizontal width of x_0 to x_1 and x_1 to x_2 respectively. The region enclosed by the trapezoids is shaded.

section.paragraph: When we use the Trapezoidal Rule, we are in effect approximating the function $$f(x)$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{1}} \right\rbrack$$ by a linear function through the two points $$\left( {x_{0},f\left( x_{0} \right)} \right)$$ and $$\left( {x_{1},f\left( x_{1} \right)} \right)$$ and the function $$f(x)$$ on $$\left\lbrack {x_{1},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ by a linear function through the two points $$\left( {x_{1},f\left( x_{1} \right)} \right)$$ and $$\left( {x_{2},f\left( x_{2} \right)} \right)$$ . Thus, the Trapezoidal Rule simply approximates the actual area of the region under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$x = x_{0}$$ to $$x = x_{2}$$ by the area of the region under the approximating polygonal curve (Figure 6b).

A natural extension of the preceding idea is to approximate portions of the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ by means of portions of the graphs of second-degree polynomials (parts of parabolas). It can be shown that given any three noncollinear points, there is a unique parabola that passes through the given points. Choose the points $$\left( {x_{0},f\left( x_{0} \right)} \right)$$ , $$\left( {x_{1},f\left( x_{1} \right)} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {x_{2},f\left( x_{2} \right)} \right)$$ corresponding to the first three points of the partition. Then we can approximate the function $$f(x)$$ on $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ by means of a quadratic function whose graph contains these three points (Figure 7).

The horizontal axis y is unlabeled. The parabola which is symmetrical about the tick mark x_0 in the x axis enters from the second quadrant cuts the y axis and opens up in the first quadrant. The curve then inflects and slopes to the right, concave up, increasing to the right cuts the parabola at (x_1, f (x_1)), further the curve slopes upward above the parabola, inflects to cut the parabola at (x_2, f (x_2)) and continues to slope upward to the right away from the parabola. A perpendicular is dropped to the x axis from the coordinates (x_0, f(x_0)), (x_1, f(x_1)), and (x_2, f(x_2)) each to the x axis, forming two trapezoids in the region below the parabola, with a horizontal width of x_0 to x_1 and x_1 to x_2 respectively. The region enclosed by the trapezoids is shaded.

figure.caption: Simpson’s Rule approximates the area of the region under the curve by the area of the region under the parabola.

section.paragraph: Although we will not do so here, it can be shown that the area of the region under the parabola between $$x = x_{0}$$ and $$x = x_{2}$$ is given by
$$\frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{0} \right) + 4f\left( x_{1} \right) + f\left( x_{2} \right)} \right\rbrack$$

Repeating this argument on the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{2},x_{4}} \right\rbrack$$ , we see that the area of the region under the curve between $$x = x_{2}$$ and $$x = x_{4}$$ is approximated by the area of the region under the parabola between $$x_{2}$$ and $$x_{4}$$ —that is, by
$$\frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{3} \right) + f\left( x_{4} \right)} \right\rbrack$$

Proceeding, we conclude that if $$n$$ is even (Why?), then the area of the region under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ may be approximated by the sum of the areas of the regions under the $$n \slash 2$$ approximating parabolas—that is,

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{0} \right) + 4f\left( x_{1} \right) + f\left( x_{2} \right)} \right\rbrack + \frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{3} \right) + f\left( x_{4} \right)} \right\rbrack + \cdots + \frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{n - 2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{n - 1} \right) + f\left( x_{n} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ { = \frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{0} \right) + 4f\left( x_{1} \right) + f\left( x_{2} \right) + f\left( x_{2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{3} \right) + f\left( x_{4} \right) + \cdots + f\left( x_{n - 2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{n - 1} \right) + f\left( x_{n} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ { = \frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{0} \right) + 4f\left( x_{1} \right) + 2f\left( x_{2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{3} \right) + 2f\left( x_{4} \right) + \cdots + 4f\left( x_{n - 1} \right) + f\left( x_{n} \right)} \right\rbrack} \end{array}$$
The preceding is the derivation of the approximation formula known as Simpson’s Rule.

note.heading: Simpson’s Rule
note.paragraph: $$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx \approx \frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{0} \right) + 4f\left( x_{1} \right) + 2f\left( x_{2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{3} \right) + 2f\left( x_{4} \right) + \cdots + 4f\left( x_{n - 1} \right) + f\left( x_{n} \right)} \right\rbrack}$$
where $$\Delta x = \frac{b - a}{n}$$ and $$n$$ is even.

section.heading: Error Analysis
section.paragraph: The following results give the bounds on the errors incurred when the Trapezoidal Rule and Simpson’s Rule are used to approximate a definite integral (proof omitted).

note.source_type: Errors in the Trapezoidal and Simpson Approximations

note.heading: Errors in the Trapezoidal and Simpson Approximations

list.item: The maximum error incurred in using the Trapezoidal Rule is (8) $$\frac{M\left( {b - a} \right)^{3}}{12n^{2}}$$ where $$M$$ is a number such that $$\left| {f^{''}{(x)|}} \right. \leq M$$ for all $$x$$ in $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .

The maximum error incurred in using Simpson’s Rule is (9) $$\frac{M\left( {b - a} \right)^{5}}{180n^{4}}$$ where $$M$$ is a number such that $$\left| {f^{(4)}\left. (x) \right|} \right. \leq M$$ for all $$x$$ in $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .

note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: In many instances, the actual error is less than the upper error bounds given.

example.heading: Example 6

is approximated by using (a) the Trapezoidal Rule and (b) Simpson’s Rule with $$n = 10$$ . Compare these with the actual errors found in Examples 1 and 3.
example.heading: Solution

list.item: Here, $$a = 1$$ , $$b = 2$$ , and $$f(x) = 1 \slash x$$ Next, to find a value for $$M$$ , we compute $$f^{\prime}(x) = - \frac{1}{x^{2}}$$ and $$f^{''}(x) = \frac{2}{x^{3}}$$ Since $$f^{''}(x)$$ is positive and decreasing on $$(1,2)$$ (Why?), it attains its maximum value of $$2$$ at $$x = 1$$ , the left endpoint of the interval. Therefore, if we take $$M = 2$$ , then $$\left| {f^{''}{(x)|}} \right. \leq 2$$ . Using (8), we see that the maximum error incurred is $$\frac{2\left( {2 - 1} \right)^{3}}{12(10)^{2}} = \frac{2}{1200} = 0.0016667$$ The actual error found in Example 1, $$0.000624$$ , is much less than the upper bound just found.

We compute $$f^{'''}(x) = \frac{- 6}{x^{4}}$$ and $$f^{(4)}{(x)} = \frac{24}{x^{5}}$$ Since $$f^{(4)}(x)$$ is positive and decreasing on $$(1,2)$$ (just look at $$f^{(5)}$$ to verify this fact), it attains its maximum at the left endpoint of $$\lbrack 1,2\rbrack$$ . Now, $$f^{(4)}(1) = 24$$ so we may take $$M = 24$$ . Using (9), we obtain the maximum error of $$\frac{24\left( {2 - 1} \right)^{5}}{180(10)^{4}} = 0.0000133$$ The actual error is $$0.000003$$ (see Example 3).
